2.title: Why we spend
2.html:
Stage 5 · Main input

Why we spend

Buy Nothing Day, and the guilt of a good deal.

Before you read: one day a year, some people ask everybody to buy absolutely nothing.

Could you go twenty-four hours without spending any money? Decide first, then read.

There is no right answer. This is your prediction — check at the end whether the text changed your mind.

Why we spend

One day a year, a small group of people stand in the busiest shops in the country and buy absolutely nothing. They think the rest of us should try it.

AEvery November the shops fill up. Prices fall, the windows say HALF-PRICE, and for a few days the whole country seems to be shopping. Some people queue outside the doors all night in the run-up to Christmas. Others buy on credit and only understand what they have spent when the bill arrives in January. In Britain alone, shoppers spend around nine billion pounds in that single week.

BThen, on the busiest shopping day of the year, a small group of people stand in the same shopping centres holding signs. They are not buying anything. It is Buy Nothing Day, and they want the rest of us to stop for twenty-four hours and think. The movement started in Canada in 1992 and now appears in more than sixty-five countries.

C“We believe shopping makes us happy,” says Lewis Castle, who has been part of the movement since 2013. “It doesn’t. Look at what happens afterwards.” He means the money people owe, and he means the planet: the richest fifth of the world’s population consumes far more than its fair share of the world’s resources, and moving goods around the world by air is one of the most harmful parts of the whole system.

DShops understand exactly how a bargain feels. A special offer does not simply mean a lower price; it means you were clever. Researchers who study consumer behaviour call this the deal effect, and it explains something strange: people come home with items they do not need, feel briefly pleased, and admit weeks later that they never wanted them at all. What follows has a plainer name. Guilt.

EGuilt sells too. The current trend is guilt-free brands — a phone you can repair, a shirt made by workers who are paid properly, a coffee that promises to protect the forest it came from. Some shoppers are convinced this is real progress, and it is not hard to see why: a company that publishes what it pays its workers is doing something its competitors are not. Others think it is an excuse. Buy the guilt-free version, they argue, and you never have to ask the harder question.

FThat question is not what you buy. It is why. Castle does not tell anybody to stop shopping for ever, and he does not pretend that one day in November changes anything. He says something much smaller and, he thinks, more useful. For twenty-four hours, you notice how often your hand goes to your pocket — and you find out how much of it you actually wanted.

Written for this course. Figures on consumption and household debt are drawn from published UN Environment Programme and OECD reporting.

5.title: Too good to be true
5.html:
Stage 5 · Main input

Too good to be true

Three famous hoaxes, and how each of them came apart.

Before you read: you will read about three stories that turned out to be false.

Which do you think spread fastest?

Decide first. The text answers this directly in the last two paragraphs.

Too good to be true

Three stories that millions of people believed. One took forty years to unravel; another lasted a single afternoon.

AIn December 1912 a lawyer named Charles Dawson announced that he had found something remarkable in a gravel pit in the south of England: a skull with a human forehead and an ape-like jaw. Scientists were keen to find evidence that would prove the link between early man and apes, and here it was. The find was reported around the world. Museums put it on display. It was named Piltdown Man.

BBy the time the hoax was discovered, scientists had wasted nearly forty years believing a lie. In 1953 a team of researchers tested the bones properly and reached an uncomfortable conclusion: the skull was human and modern, the jaw belonged to an orangutan, and the teeth had been filed down and stained to match. Meanwhile Dawson, who most people now consider responsible for making the fake, had died. Nobody was ever charged.

CNot every hoax takes forty years. On 15 October 2009 the media reported that a six-year-old boy was inside a large silver balloon floating high in the sky above Colorado. The police were informed and helicopters were sent up to track it. By the time the balloon finally landed about eighty kilometres away, an hour or so later, the story was live on television and millions of people were watching.

DThe boy was not in the balloon. He was at home, hiding in the family garage. That evening, while reporters were interviewing the family on live television, he accidentally mentioned that they had done it “for the show”. The whole story had been made up by his parents in an attempt to get a reality TV deal. As soon as the interview ended, the police reopened the case.

EHoaxes travel faster than they used to. Before the internet, a false story needed a newspaper. Now a picture circulates in minutes: a bright blue watermelon that supposedly changes the taste of everything you eat afterwards, or a claim that dialling the emergency number will charge your phone battery. That second one caused real harm. Police announced that calls to 999 had risen sharply, and told the public to ignore the hoax and keep the line free.

FSo why do we believe? Researchers who study this point to two things. First, a good hoax gives people what they already expect — Piltdown Man arrived exactly when scientists were looking for it. Second, checking takes effort, and sharing takes none. Until that changes, the next story that seems too good to be true will still reach a few million screens before anyone thinks to ask.

Written for this course. The Piltdown Man, Loch Ness and balloon-boy cases are documented in the archives of the Natural History Museum, London, and in contemporary news reporting.

7.title: The marshmallow test
7.html:
Stage 5 · Main input

The marshmallow test

The experiment, and what it really predicted.

Before you read: four-year-olds were offered one marshmallow now, or two if they could wait fifteen minutes.

What proportion of the children do you think managed to wait?

Decide first. Paragraph A gives you the answer.

The children who waited

A test with a marshmallow seemed to predict how children’s lives would turn out. Fifty years later, researchers are still arguing about what it really measured.

AThe experiment could not have been simpler. A researcher put a marshmallow on a plate in front of a four-year-old and made a promise. “If you can be patient and wait until I come back, you can have two.” Then he left the room. What happened next was filmed, and the films are still difficult to watch: children who could not resist covered their eyes, turned their backs, sang to themselves, and sat on their hands. Most of them gave in before the fifteen minutes were up.

BThe psychologist behind it, Walter Mischel, began this work at Stanford University around 1970. He was not really interested in marshmallows. He wanted to measure something much harder to see: whether a small child could hold on to a reward that was not there yet. The successful children were not the ones who stared at the plate and made an enormous effort. They were the ones who managed to turn their attention away from it — and if you succeed in doing that, Mischel argued, you may forget about the temptation altogether.

CYears later, his team went back to the same children, who were now teenagers. The results were striking. Those who had been able to wait longer had better exam results, coped better with stress, and were described by their parents as more socially confident. The study became one of the most famous experiments in psychology, and its conclusion spread far beyond the laboratory: teach children to wait, and you improve their lives.

DThen, in 2018, a team led by Tyler Watts repeated the study with a much larger and more varied group of children. They found something more complicated. Children who waited did tend to do better later — but once the researchers took the family’s income and education into account, most of the difference disappeared. A child from a secure home has good reasons to trust a promise. A child who has learned that promised things often do not arrive has good reasons to eat the marshmallow now.

EThis does not mean the original experiment was worthless. It was probably measuring two things at once: the ability to resist, and the experience that makes resisting seem sensible. In one version of the test, researchers deliberately broke a promise to one group of children before the marshmallow appeared. Those children waited, on average, about a third as long as the others. They had not become less patient. They had simply stopped believing the researcher.

FSo what should we take from it? Not that some children are born to succeed and others are not. Mischel himself always insisted that waiting is a technique rather than a personality: you can teach a child to look away, to think about something else, to make a plan. What the newer research adds is a second, less comfortable point. Before you can ask a child to wait for a reward, somebody has to make sure the reward actually comes.

Written for this course. Based on published accounts of Walter Mischel’s Stanford experiments (from 1970) and on Watts, Duncan and Quan, Psychological Science, 2018.

8.title: Faking it
8.html:
Stage 5 · Main input

Faking it

Four weeks to learn a job, and a panel of judges who have to spot the beginner.

Before you read: a television programme trains people with no experience for four weeks, then asks professionals to spot them.

What do you think gives the fakes away?

Choose one. Paragraph E tells you what the judges actually say.

Faking it

A television programme sends people with no experience into a job for four weeks, then asks a panel of professionals to spot them. What separates the ones who survive from the ones who don’t is rarely what you would expect.

AThe idea behind the programme is simple and slightly cruel. Producers take somebody with no experience in a particular job — a chef, a chauffeur, a fitness instructor — and give them four weeks with an expert. At the end, they must take part in a contest against real professionals, and a panel of judges has to decide which one is faking it. If the judges cannot tell, the newcomer wins.

BEd worked in a burger van before the programme found him. He had to be reliable and turn up for work on time; he had to be reasonably pleasant to customers; and that, more or less, was the job. He did not have to take much responsibility, because his boss dealt with the money. Four weeks later he was expected to run a professional kitchen. “Nobody tells you,” he said afterwards, “that in a real kitchen you must work to very precise times. Thirty seconds is a long time.”

CThis is where most candidates struggle, and it is not usually the technical skill that defeats them. You can teach somebody to crack an egg, flip it and get it onto a plate. You cannot teach them, in four weeks, to multitask under pressure while five other people are shouting. A chef must plan several dishes at once, hold the whole schedule in their head, and think ahead constantly. Candidates who set goals for each shift tend to survive; those who simply react do not.

DThe social rules are just as hard. Ed was shocked to realise that he could not say please and thank you all the time if he wanted the team to respect him — in a busy kitchen, a short instruction is not rudeness, it is efficiency. In other jobs the opposite applies. A chauffeur may not start a conversation with a passenger unless the passenger starts it first, and is not allowed to comment on anything they overhear. Every workplace has rules like these, and none of them are written down anywhere.

EJudges say the giveaway is almost never a technical mistake. It is confidence in the wrong place: the candidate who explains too much, apologises too often, or checks the time. One judge put it bluntly. “A professional does not have to think about how they look. That is the difference, and you can see it in about ninety seconds.”

FPerhaps the most useful thing the programme reveals is what a job actually consists of. We describe work in terms of qualifications and technique, but for four weeks these candidates discover something else: that most of a job is behaviour. You have to know when to speak, when to be quiet, what you are allowed to touch, and what nobody will ever explain to you. Some of them go back to their old lives afterwards. A surprising number do not.

Written for this course. The format described is based on documented reality-television ‘job swap’ programmes broadcast in the UK and elsewhere.

10.title: Living on the water
10.html:
Stage 5 · Main input

Living on the water

A family whose home floats, and what they think happens next.

Before you read: in several countries, people are building permanent homes on water.

Why do you think they do it?

Choose one. The text gives more than one reason — see how many you find.

Living on the water

Around the world, people are moving off the land — not because they want an adventure, but because the land is running out.

AOn Lake Titicaca, high in the Andes, there are islands you can pull apart with your hands. The Uros people build them from reeds, layer on layer, and add fresh reeds on top every few weeks as the bottom rots away. A well-kept island will last about thirty years. There are no cliffs, no rocks and no valleys here — just a flat green landscape that moves slightly underfoot, and about two thousand inhabitants who have lived this way for centuries.

BFour thousand miles away, in Amsterdam, a very different community is doing something similar for very modern reasons. The city has run out of space. Prices in the suburbs are impossible, and moving inland is not an option, so about a hundred households have settled down on the water instead. Their homes are permanent and connected to the city like any other: post, internet, solar power on the roof.

CMarijke has lived on one of them for six years. “People think we are going to feel cramped, packed in like sardines,” she says. “Come and look.” Inside, the rooms are ordinary; there is a communal garden shared by the whole block and a thirty-minute ferry service to the mainland. “The one thing you learn is to make room. Everything you own has to earn its place. I’ll never go back to a house with an attic full of things I have forgotten about.”

DNot everybody is convinced. Building on water is expensive, and critics argue that the money will always go where the profit is. In the Maldives, a company is developing artificial islands to provide housing for the country’s poorer citizens, and by 2030 it expects twenty thousand people to be living there. Others say the same technology will end up producing luxury housing for people who could live anywhere they liked.

EWhat is certain is that the pressure is not going to disappear. By 2050, roughly two thirds of the world’s population will live in cities, and a large number of the biggest ones sit on a coast or a river. Some of them will build upwards. Some will build outwards, into the suburbs. A few, planners think, will build onto the water — not as an experiment, but because there will be nowhere else to put people.

FMarijke is more modest about it. She did not set off six years ago to solve a global problem; she wanted a home she could afford within reach of her work. “I don’t think everyone is going to live like this,” she says. “But you get used to it very fast. After about a month, you stop noticing that the floor is moving. And then it is just where you live.”

Written for this course. Details of the Uros islands, the Amsterdam floating districts and the Maldives project are drawn from published municipal planning documents and UNESCO reporting.

13.title: A film that travels
13.html:
Stage 5 · Main input

A film that travels

Why some stories work everywhere, and expensive ones often do not.

Before you read: some films are watched all over the world, and others never leave the country that made them.

What do you think matters most?

Decide first. Paragraph C answers this directly.

A film that travels

Some films cross borders effortlessly. Others, made with far more money, stop at the first subtitle. What is the difference?

AIn 2019, a South Korean film about a poor family and a rich one won the biggest prize in world cinema. Its director had a warning for audiences who avoid foreign films: once you get over the one-inch barrier of subtitles, he said, you will find many more films worth watching. The remark stuck, because it named something the industry has always known. Most films never leave home, and the reason is rarely the quality of the plot.

BNigeria produces more films than almost anywhere on earth. The industry there tends to work fast and cheaply, and it has an audience that stretches far beyond Nigeria: its fans log in from Brazil, India and the United States. Producers have learned to showcase African culture to the world rather than to imitate Hollywood, and audiences seem to enjoy watching stories they have not already seen a hundred times. A growing middle class looking for entertainment has done the rest.

CSo what travels? Not, it turns out, special effects. Distributors who study this say the films that cross borders most easily are built on a situation any audience recognises immediately: a family under pressure, a person who decides to set out on a journey, somebody who wants to escape a life that has closed around them. The cast can be unknown and the budget small. What matters is that a viewer in another country does not need to be told why the character is doing this.

DGenre helps too, but not in the way people expect. Animated films travel well because the voices can be replaced. Thrillers travel because tension needs very few words. Comedy travels worst of all: a joke often depends on the exact way something is said, and a translator who tries to keep the meaning usually loses the timing. Romcoms sit somewhere in the middle, which is why studios keep remaking them locally instead of exporting them.

EThen there is the slow route. The Shawshank Redemption failed at the box office when it was originally released in 1994. It has since become a modern classic, largely because television kept showing it and audiences kept recommending it to each other. Its story — friendship, patience and hope inside a prison — needs no local knowledge at all. Some films do not travel in space so much as in time.

FNone of this means a film must be simple. Audiences are perfectly willing to work; what they are not willing to do is work without a reason. A film that gives them a character worth following will hold them for two hours in any language. A film that does not will be switched off in ten minutes, however stunning the photography is.

Written for this course. Box-office and industry figures are drawn from published reporting on the Nigerian film industry and on international distribution.

16.title: The car that drives itself
16.html:
Stage 5 · Main input

The car that drives itself

The machines are already here. The argument is about something else.

Before you read: cars that drive themselves are already on the road in several countries.

What do you think is the hardest part for the engineers?

Choose one, then check Paragraph C.

The car that drives itself

The technology that removes the driver is already on the road. The hard part was never the driving.

AThere is a figure that appears in almost every discussion of driverless cars, and it explains why so much money has gone into them: around ninety per cent of road accidents are caused by human error. More than a million people die on the roads every year. A machine that never gets tired, never looks at its phone and never misjudges a gap at a junction would, in theory, remove most of that.

BMuch of the technology is already here, and you may be using it. Cars which brake automatically when the gap ahead closes are now ordinary. So are cars that park themselves, and systems which warn a driver who is slipping out of the correct lane on a motorway. Each of these does one job. What engineers call full automation — a vehicle that can handle any road, in any weather, with nobody paying attention — is a different problem altogether.

CThe difficulty is not the driving. It is the small number of situations that a human handles without noticing and a machine cannot. A ball rolls into the road, which usually means a child will follow. A police officer waves you through a red light. Two drivers arrive at a narrow gap at the same moment and settle it with a look. Engineers describe these as edge cases, and the awkward truth is that there is no complete list of them.

DFor some people the argument is already settled. Neil, who has had a disability since birth, will never take a driving test. “People talk about losing control,” he says. “I have never had it. A car that drives itself is the one possession that would change my week, and it is not replaceable by anything else. When people tell me the technology is not perfect yet, my answer is: neither is the system we have now.”

EThere are losses as well as gains, and they are not evenly shared. Driving is one of the most common paid occupations in many countries. If the vehicles that carry goods across a country no longer need a person in the cab, a large number of people whose skills are difficult to transfer will be looking for work. Some economists think new jobs will appear; others point out that they rarely appear in the same places, or for the same people.

FSo the question that matters is probably not whether the technology will arrive. It is what we decide to do while it does. The countries which are already writing rules for testing, insurance and responsibility will shape how it is used. The ones which wait will get whatever the manufacturers give them — which, as Neil points out, is roughly how the current system was built in the first place.

Written for this course. Collision-cause statistics and the levels-of-automation framework are drawn from published road-safety research and international engineering standards.

19.title: The way we used to work
19.html:
Stage 5 · Main input

The way we used to work

Forty-one years in one building, and what was gained and lost.

Before you read: working life has changed enormously in the last fifty years.

Which change do you think matters most?

Choose one. The text discusses all three — see which one it ends on.

The way we used to work

Fifty years ago, most people expected one employer, one office and one pension. Almost every part of that has gone.

AThere was a time when a young person would leave school, walk into a local firm and stay there. My grandfather worked for the same company for forty-one years. He used to say that changing jobs looked unreliable — that an employer would want to know why you had left. The average worker today changes employer roughly every four to five years, and nobody asks that question any more.

BSome occupations have disappeared entirely. Before alarm clocks were cheap, British factory towns employed knocker-uppers, who would walk the streets before dawn tapping on bedroom windows with a long stick until the sleeper appeared. Large offices had typing pools, where thirty or forty women would sit in rows typing what other people had written. Telegram boys, lift operators, lamplighters: none of these jobs was unskilled, and none of them exists now.

CThe working day was different too, and not always in the direction people imagine. Hours were long, but the boundaries were solid. When my grandfather left the building, he had left. There was no way for the office to reach him, and nobody expected it to. He used to describe his working conditions as hard but simple: you obeyed the rules, you followed the procedures, and in return the firm was supposed to look after you until you retired.

DWhat replaced it is more relaxed and much less certain. Dress codes have almost gone. Many people can work from home, choose their own hours, or take a temporary contract that suits a particular year of their life. But the promise on the other side of that arrangement has gone as well. Very few employers now offer anything that resembles a lifetime, and the person who used to be looked after is expected to manage their own training, their own pension and their own reputation.

EWhether this is progress depends on where you stand. People with skills that are in demand have never had more freedom: they can quit, negotiate, retrain or move country. People without them have inherited the insecurity without the freedom. The same change produced both outcomes, which is why arguments about modern work so often talk past each other.

FMy grandfather, who lived long enough to see the beginning of all this, was not nostalgic about it. He would point out that his forty-one years were not really a choice; there was nothing else, and leaving was frightening. “You had one life and one job,” he said, “and you hoped they suited each other.” What he valued was not the job. It was knowing, at twenty-five, roughly what the next forty years would look like — and that, more than any occupation, is what has actually disappeared.

22.title: The happiest country in the world
22.html:
Stage 5 · Main input

The happiest country in the world

Denmark keeps winning. The reasons are not the ones people expect.

Before you read: a yearly report ranks countries by how satisfied their people say they are.

What do you think matters most?

Decide first. The last paragraph gives the researchers’ answer.

The happiest country in the world

Every year a report ranks the world by happiness, and every year the same small northern countries come out on top. The interesting part is not who wins. It is why.

ASince 2012, researchers have asked people in more than 150 countries a deceptively simple question. Imagine a ladder with ten steps. The top step is the best possible life for you; the bottom is the worst. Which step are you standing on today? The answers are averaged, and the result is published as the World Happiness Report. The Nordic countries have finished at or near the top almost every year since it began.

BThe obvious explanation is money, and it is partly right. If a country is very poor, its people report low satisfaction, and that changes quickly when incomes rise. But the relationship breaks down higher up the scale. Above a certain point, extra income makes surprisingly little difference. If a society is already comfortable, what raises satisfaction is not a bigger economy but a fairer one — and a lower gap between the richest and the poorest predicts happiness better than the national income does.

CSo the researchers look at six factors: income, healthy life expectancy, social support, freedom to make your own choices, generosity, and trust. That last one does most of the work. If you believe a lost wallet in your city would be returned to you, you will report a higher life satisfaction — and in the Nordic countries, unusually, most people do believe it. Denmark has repeatedly come near the top of that particular measure.

DWhat does this look like day to day? Free or very cheap childcare, so that having a child does not end a career. Healthcare that does not depend on your employer. Reasonable working hours: people tend to have more job satisfaction if they finish at a sensible time, and Danes spend a good deal of their leisure time socializing rather than working. Then there is hygge, a word with no exact English translation, which describes a particular cosy, unhurried kind of evening with friends and family.

ENone of this makes the model easy to copy, and it is not free. Taxes are high, and the whole arrangement depends on a level of trust in public institutions that takes generations to build and can be lost quickly. Critics also point out that the survey measures how content people say they are, not how content they are. If a culture is uncomfortable with complaining, its scores will look good whatever is really happening.

FPerhaps the most useful finding is the least glamorous. Across every country studied, the strongest single predictor of satisfaction is not wealth, weather or health, but whether people feel they have somebody to rely on in a crisis. Unless you have that, very little else compensates — and provided you do, a great deal can be survived. It is not a policy that any government can simply announce, which may be exactly why it is so often ignored.

Written for this course. Rankings and factors are drawn from the World Happiness Report, published annually by the UN Sustainable Development Solutions Network.

25.title: How would you describe them?
25.html:
Stage 5 · Main input

How would you describe them?

Two drawings of the same face, and only one of them looks like a stranger did it.

Before you read: two portraits were drawn of the same face — one from the woman’s own description, one from a stranger’s.

Which do you think looked better?

Decide first. Paragraph B tells you what happened.

How would you describe them?

A forensic artist drew two portraits of the same woman. He never saw her. The difference between the two pictures became one of the most-watched advertisements ever made.

AThe set-up was unusual. A forensic artist — the kind normally employed by the police to draw a suspect from a witness’s description — sat behind a curtain. He could not see the woman on the other side. She described her own face to him: shoulder-length hair, a fringe, a rather large chin. He drew what he heard. Then a stranger who had met her that morning described the same face, and he drew it again.

BThe two portraits were put side by side. Almost every time, the self-described face was older, heavier and sadder than the one the stranger described. One woman had called her own face “a lot more closed off, and fatter, sadder too”. The stranger’s version had softer eyes and a slightly open mouth. The women were shown both drawings together, and several of them cried.

CThe film went round the world within days, and psychologists were quick to point out that it was not an experiment. The women were not chosen at random, the strangers were prompted to be kind, and a commercial company paid for all of it. None of that, though, explains why the film worked. It worked because the gap it showed was one almost everybody recognises: we are far more precise about our own faults than about anybody else’s.

DResearch on self-perception supports the general point, if not the advertisement. People describing themselves use noticeably more negative detail than people describing a stranger. They are also far more specific: a double chin, thin eyebrows, a nose that is slightly crooked. Strangers describe in much broader strokes — blonde, quite slim, well-built, friendly-looking — and rarely mention the features that the person themselves has been thinking about for twenty years.

ESome of this is simply information. You have looked at your own face many thousands of times more often than anyone else has, so you notice smaller changes: the grey coming in, the hair going. A stranger has three seconds and a general impression. It is not that they are being generous. They are working with far less detail, and detail is where dissatisfaction lives.

FThe advertisement ended with a line telling women they were more beautiful than they thought. It is a nice sentiment, and it is also a company selling soap. The more interesting conclusion is smaller and harder to package: the face other people see is not more flattering than yours. It is simply less examined — and by far the most critical description of you that exists anywhere is the one you carry around in your own head.

Written for this course. Based on published accounts of the Real Beauty Sketches campaign (2013) and on research into self-perception.

28.title: The crowd will pay for it
28.html:
Stage 5 · Main input

The crowd will pay for it

Products used to be made and then sold. Now it is the other way round.

Before you read: crowd-funding lets people pay for a product before it exists.

What proportion of projects do you think reach their target?

Decide first. Paragraph D gives the figure.

The crowd will pay for it

A hat that lets you sleep at your desk raised nearly two hundred thousand dollars from strangers. Most projects are not so lucky.

AThe Ostrich Pillow was invented to solve a problem that no bank would have taken seriously. Its designer had noticed that people who travel a lot get very tired, and that there is nowhere to put your head. The result is a padded hat that is pulled over the head so that the wearer can take a nap almost anywhere. It looks ridiculous, which is part of the point. More than nineteen hundred people paid for one before a single unit had been manufactured.

BThis is how crowd-funding works. An idea is presented directly to the people who might buy it, usually as a short film and a page of drawings. Money is pledged rather than paid: nothing is taken from anyone unless the target is reached by the deadline. If it is, the money is released and production begins. If it is not, every pledge is returned and the project quietly disappears. Nothing is guaranteed to anybody at any stage.

CFor a designer who is short of cash, the attraction is obvious. A bank loan must be applied for, defended and repaid whatever happens; a crowd-funded product is paid for by the people who actually want it. But the real value is often information rather than money. If two thousand strangers will pay in advance for something that does not yet exist, the idea has been tested before a factory is booked. If only forty will, that is worth knowing too, and it has cost almost nothing to find out.

DThe failure rate is high and is not usually mentioned in the success stories. Only around a third of projects reach their target, and reaching it is not the end of the difficulty. Products that were designed in a bedroom have to be manufactured, packed and shipped to thousands of addresses in dozens of countries, often by people who have never done any of that before. Deliveries are regularly delayed by a year or more, and backers are told about the problem long after they were told about the triumph.

EPlatforms have been criticised for this. Their defenders answer that a pledge is not a purchase: backers are supporting an attempt, not ordering from a shop, and that distinction is printed clearly on every page. Critics reply that it is not how the pages are read, and that a page filled with photographs of a finished-looking product is understood as an advertisement whatever the small print says.

FWhat has genuinely changed is who gets to try. Fifty years ago an unusual idea had to be presented to somebody with money, and most such ideas were refused by people who were paid to be careful. Now they are refused, or backed, by the public. The Ostrich Pillow was rejected by every manufacturer its designer approached. Then it was funded in three weeks by strangers, and has since been sold in more than fifty countries.

Written for this course. Platform mechanics and success rates are drawn from published crowd-funding platform statistics and industry reporting.

31.title: The last outlaw
31.html:
Stage 5 · Main input

The last outlaw

Five aircraft, sixty thousand followers, and a road not taken.

Before you read: a nineteen-year-old stole aircraft he had never been trained to fly, and became an internet celebrity.

Why do you think people supported him?

Decide first. Paragraph C gives the writer’s answer.

The last outlaw

For two years a teenager stole planes, boats and cars across North America, and thousands of strangers cheered him on. Almost nobody asked what the people he robbed thought about it.

AThe police called him a suspect in more than a hundred thefts. The internet called him the barefoot bandit, because he often carried out his robberies with no shoes on, and because a photograph of bare footprints on a stolen floor is a better story than a list of charges. A Facebook page collecting support for him gathered tens of thousands of likes. Somebody wrote a song. He was nineteen, and he had reportedly taught himself to fly using information he found online.

BThe flying is what turned a local crime story into an international one. Between 2008 and 2010 he took at least five light aircraft, none of which he had ever been trained to operate, and crash-landed every one. He was finally captured in the Bahamas after flying a stolen plane more than a thousand miles from Indiana, running it out of fuel, and putting it down in shallow water. None of his victims were injured. That fact did a great deal of work in the way the story was told.

CIt is not difficult to see why people enjoyed it. The story had a shape that audiences already knew: a young man alone, technically skilled, taking from people who could afford the loss and hurting nobody. If he had used violence even once, the Facebook page would have emptied overnight. If anyone had been hurt in one of those landings, there would have been no song.

DThe people he stole from tell it differently. He did not only take aircraft. He broke into houses and small businesses in a rural area where a stolen boat is somebody’s income and an insurance claim takes months. One shop owner described lying awake listening to noises for a year afterwards. “They made him into a film,” she said. “Nobody made a film about the year I spent frightened in my own house.”

EThe court took a view somewhere between the two. He was sentenced to seven years, and the judge accepted that a childhood of extraordinary neglect was part of the explanation, though not an excuse. An unusual condition was attached to the sentence: any money made from the film rights would go straight to his victims. It was an attempt to correct, in a small way, the thing the case had exposed — that the story was worth far more than the damage was.

FPerhaps the most uncomfortable question is not about him at all. If the same teenager had broken into the same houses without ever getting into a plane, nobody outside the county would have heard his name. He would have been an ordinary burglar with a difficult history, and he would have served his sentence unnoticed. The flying did not change what he took. It changed who was willing to watch.

Written for this course. Based on contemporary court reporting and published accounts of the case of Colton Harris-Moore (2008–2010).

35.title: How to change someone’s mind
35.html:
Stage 5 · Main input

How to change someone’s mind

The people who are best at it are the ones who talk least.

Before you read: researchers have tested what actually changes somebody’s mind.

Which do you think works best?

Choose one. Paragraphs A and C give the research answer.

How to change someone's mind

Almost everything we instinctively do in an argument makes the other person less likely to agree. The research on this is unusually consistent, and unusually ignored.

AAsk people how to win an argument and most will describe the same method: gather the strongest facts, present them clearly, and wait for the other side to see sense. Researchers who study persuasion asked whether this works. In several studies, giving people accurate information that contradicted a firmly held belief produced no change at all, and in some cases the belief grew stronger. The listeners had not failed to understand the evidence. They had understood it and defended themselves against it.

BOne reason is that beliefs are rarely stored on their own. A view about a political question is usually attached to a group of people, a set of experiences and a sense of who you are. Attack the view directly and the person hears something larger being attacked, so they do what anybody does under attack: they hold on harder. This is why an argument between two well-informed people so often ends with both of them more certain than when they started.

CSo what does work? The most striking evidence comes from a technique in which trained volunteers knock on doors and, instead of arguing, ask questions. They ask whether the person has ever known anybody in the situation being discussed. Then they listen, without correcting anything, for ten or fifteen minutes. In controlled trials this approach produced measurable shifts in opinion that were still there weeks later — far more than a leaflet full of facts achieved.

DProfessional negotiators arrived at something similar from a different direction. One of them, who has spent his career teaching this, says that people ask him how to overcome objections and are disappointed by his answer. You do not overcome an objection, he tells them; you make sure the other person believes you have understood it. He advises repeating the objection back in your own words and asking whether you have got it right, and he claims that people will often argue themselves halfway towards you while you are still listening.

EThere is a warning attached to all of this. The techniques that genuinely change minds are the same ones used by people whose intentions are not good, and they work faster on those who are tired, frightened or alone. Nothing in the research says that a mind changed by careful listening has been changed towards the truth. It says only that it has been changed — which is a reason to notice when it is happening to you.

FWhat almost nobody wants to hear is how slow the honest version is. A leaflet costs pennies and reaches thousands. A conversation costs twenty minutes and reaches one person. Every organisation that has to persuade people at scale is aware of this arithmetic, and most of them choose the leaflet, knowing what the evidence says. Persuasion, it turns out, is not difficult to understand. It is difficult to afford.

Written for this course. Based on published work on persuasion and attitude change, including studies of the backfire effect and of deep canvassing.
